title: Arterial blood gas interpretation in a surgical patient

header.contentArea: Applied surgical science and critical care

related.why: The same patient group and the decision to operate
Reading a blood gas alongside the electrolytes

brief.scenario: Mr Colin Ashby, 68, was admitted yesterday with adhesional small bowel obstruction after a previous laparotomy. He has vomited repeatedly and is being managed non-operatively with a nasogastric tube and IV fluids.
brief.task: The examiner will show you his arterial blood gases in stages. Interpret each one systematically and say what you would do.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Oxygenation, pH, PaCO2, bicarbonate, compensation, anion gap, lactate; then act.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Calling the second gas 'compensated' and carrying on with drip and suck.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "First, what was his inspired oxygen when this was taken?"

grid.label: Systematic read and oxygenation
grid.fail: Jumps to a diagnosis without a sequence, or reads PaO2 without asking the FiO2.
grid.pass: Asks the FiO2; PaO2 11.2 kPa on air is normal (10.67–13.33); then pH, PaCO2, bicarbonate, base excess, compensation, anion gap, lactate.
grid.high: States each normal range as used, and reads the electrolytes on the same sample.

grid.label: Gas 1: metabolic alkalosis
grid.fail: Calls it respiratory, or misses the alkalosis.
grid.pass: pH 7.50 and bicarbonate 37: metabolic alkalosis, with a raised PaCO2 of 6.4 kPa as respiratory compensation.
grid.high: Notes compensation never fully normalises the pH, and base excess +13 confirms the metabolic cause.

grid.label: Gas 1: cause and treatment
grid.fail: Doesn't link it to vomiting, or ignores the potassium.
grid.pass: Vomiting and nasogastric loss of acid; potassium 3.0 is low; rehydrate and replace potassium, measuring NG losses.
grid.high: Explains dehydration keeps the kidney retaining bicarbonate, so rehydration corrects it faster; checks renal function for AKI.

grid.label: Gas 2: high anion gap metabolic acidosis
grid.fail: Misses the acidosis, or calls it compensated.
grid.pass: pH 7.28, bicarbonate 13.5, PaCO2 3.9 kPa: metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation; anion gap 136 − (104 + 13.5) = 18.5, raised.
grid.high: Knows the range depends on the analyser (about 3–11 with ion-selective electrodes); sees the swing from alkalosis to acidosis as deterioration.

grid.label: Lactate and the bowel
grid.fail: Puts the lactate down to vomiting or the saline.
grid.pass: Lactate 6.8: tissue hypoperfusion; in obstruction, suspects strangulated or ischaemic bowel.
grid.high: Knows examination misses about half of strangulations, so a soft abdomen doesn't reassure.

grid.label: Sepsis and resuscitation (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Treats the numbers without seeing him, or delays antibiotics.
grid.pass: Sees him now; NEWS2 8 is high risk: IV antibiotics within 1 hour; 250 ml crystalloid boluses, up to 1,000 ml, reassessing each.
grid.high: Seeks senior advice if not improved after 1,000 ml, and calls the surgical team for source control.

grid.label: Stopping non-operative management (safety-critical)
grid.pass: Strangulation suspected: stops non-operative management; urgent CT only if it won't delay theatre.
grid.high: Names CT signs needing surgery without delay: closed loop, ischaemia, free fluid.

grid.label: Escalation and risk
grid.fail: Waits for the morning ward round.
grid.pass: Registrar and consultant now; risk of death documented by ST3 or above.
grid.high: If predicted mortality is 5% or more: consultant surgeon and anaesthetist in theatre, critical care afterwards.

high.text: On air? Then PaO2 11.2 is normal, 10.67 to 13.33. pH, PaCO2, bicarbonate and base excess, compensation, anion gap, lactate, and I'll read the electrolytes on the same sample.

high.text: pH 7.50, bicarbonate 37, base excess +13: metabolic alkalosis. PaCO2 6.4 is compensation, and as expected it hasn't normalised the pH.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Acid lost by vomiting and NG drainage; potassium 3.0. While he's dry, his kidneys hold on to bicarbonate, so rehydration and potassium correct it faster. I'd check his creatinine.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: pH 7.28, bicarbonate 13.5, PaCO2 3.9: metabolic acidosis, compensated by breathing. Anion gap, sodium minus chloride and bicarbonate, is 18.5, against the lab's range of about 3 to 11. He's swung from alkalosis to acidosis: he's deteriorating.

failures.move: Continuing drip and suck with a new acidosis and lactate 6.8.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: strangulated bowel becomes gangrenous or perforates.

failures.move: Delaying antibiotics and fluids in a patient with NEWS2 8.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: delay in a high-risk septic patient.

failures.move: Calling a pH of 7.28 'compensated' because the PaCO2 is low.
failures.consequence: The acidosis is missed and the team is falsely reassured.

failures.move: Reading the PaO2 without knowing the FiO2.
failures.consequence: Hypoxaemia on high-flow oxygen can be read as normal.

recovery.line: Let me go back to the sequence: oxygenation, pH, CO2, bicarbonate, compensation, anion gap, lactate.

recovery.when: You can't recall the normal gap
recovery.line: I'd use the lab's reference range; 18.5 is above the usual ranges.

knowledge.fact: Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO3), the usual formula. The normal range depends on the method: about 3–11 mmol/L with ion-selective electrodes. Use your lab's range.
Normal on air: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO2 4.67–6.00 kPa, PaO2 10.67–13.33 kPa, bicarbonate 23–28, base excess −2 to +2.
Vomiting and NG suction cause metabolic alkalosis; raised lactate from ischaemic bowel causes a high anion gap acidosis.
Bowel obstruction: check lactate, electrolytes and creatinine; low potassium is frequent.
NEWS2 7 or more with suspected sepsis: antibiotics within 1 hour.

recall.think: Strangulated bowel behind a new acidosis.
recall.say: "High anion gap acidosis with lactate 6.8: I suspect ischaemic bowel."
do: See him, antibiotics, fluids, senior, theatre

numbers.meaning: normal anion gap, Na − (Cl + HCO3), ion-selective electrodes; lab ranges vary

recall.trap: A low PaCO2 is compensation, not a normal gas.
recall.finish: Laparotomy for strangulation; critical care afterwards.

sources.name: RCEMLearning reference: Arterial blood gas analysis (Kelly G; ed. Kendall JM)
sources.supports: Normal values on room air: pH 7.35-7.45, pCO2 4.67-6.00 kPa, pO2 10.67-13.33 kPa, bicarbonate 23-28 mmol/L, base excess -2 to +2; raised anion gap causes include lactate from tissue hypoxia such as ischaemic bowel; metabolic alkalosis from vomiting or nasogastric suction; compensation: ventilation falls in metabolic alkalosis and rises in metabolic acidosis; rehydration corrects the alkalosis of vomiting more quickly; a normal pH does not exclude serious illness

sources.name: Kraut JA, Nagami GT. The serum anion gap in the evaluation of acid-base disorders: what are its limitations and can its effectiveness be improved? Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2013;8(11):2018-2024
sources.supports: The anion gap is most frequently calculated as Na - (Cl + HCO3), and the major textbooks leave out potassium; the normal range depends on the laboratory method (for example 7-13, or 3-11 with ion-selective electrodes, in Rose's textbook), so use the laboratory's own range; a lactic acidosis can be present with a normal anion gap

sources.name: ten Broek RPG, Krielen P, Di Saverio S, et al. Bologna guidelines for diagnosis and management of adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO): 2017 update of the evidence-based guidelines from the World Society of Emergency Surgery ASBO working group. World J Emerg Surg 2018;13:24
sources.supports: Non-operative management unless peritonitis, strangulation or ischaemia; examination detects strangulation in only 48%; minimum bloods: blood count, lactate, electrolytes, CRP, urea/creatinine; low potassium frequent and must be corrected; dehydration causes AKI; CT is the investigation of choice; closed loop, ischaemia and free fluid mean surgery without delay

sources.name: NICE NG253: Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over: recognition, assessment and early management
sources.supports: High risk = NEWS2 7 or more; IV antibiotics within 1 hour (1.8.3); 250 ml crystalloid boluses up to 1,000 ml in total (1.8.6-1.8.7); senior advice if not improved after 1,000 ml (1.8.9); early surgical team for source control (1.11.4)

sources.name: Royal College of Physicians: National Early Warning Score (NEWS) 2
sources.supports: NEWS2 parameter bands and aggregate score

sources.name: RCS England: The High-Risk General Surgical Patient: Raising the Standard
sources.supports: Standard 3: risk of death assessed and recorded by a senior surgeon (ST3 and above) within four hours of admission; standard 4: high risk = predicted hospital mortality 5% or more; standard 8: consultant surgeon and consultant anaesthetist present, and immediate postoperative critical care admission

partner.opening: Mr Ashby's first arterial gas has just come back. Please interpret it.

reveals.finding: Gas 1: pH 7.50, PaCO2 6.4 kPa, PaO2 11.2 kPa, bicarbonate 37 mmol/L, base excess +13.

reveals.trigger: Asks for electrolytes and lactate on gas 1

reveals.finding: Say: "Twelve hours later he is worse." Gas 2 on air: pH 7.28, PaCO2 3.9 kPa, PaO2 11.8 kPa, bicarbonate 13.5, base excess −12, Na 136, K 3.6, Cl 104, lactate 6.8.
RR 26, SpO2 96% on air, BP 98/58, pulse 124, alert, temperature 38.4°C: NEWS2 8.

push.question: How do you know the raised PaCO2 in gas 1 isn't a respiratory acidosis?
push.expect: pH is high and bicarbonate is high: the primary problem is metabolic alkalosis; the CO2 is compensation.

push.question: Calculate the anion gap for gas 2.
push.expect: 136 − (104 + 13.5) = 18.5; normal about 3–11 with ion-selective electrodes, but use the lab's range.

push.question: What would make you take him to theatre?
push.expect: Peritonism, strangulation or ischaemia; on CT a closed loop, ischaemia or free fluid.

curveballs.prompt: The lactate on gas 2 is 1.9. Does that reassure you?
curveballs.safeAnswer: No: the new acidosis, fever and tenderness still need urgent senior review and CT or theatre.

curveballs.prompt: Gas 2 was taken on 40% oxygen, PaO2 11.8.
curveballs.safeAnswer: That PaO2 is low for 40% oxygen: impaired oxygenation, perhaps aspiration. Assess the chest and escalate.

curveballs.prompt: The registrar asks whether to give sodium bicarbonate.
curveballs.safeAnswer: No: treat the cause with resuscitation and source control.
